Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Expectation2: Repair or replace damaged wooden structures or components
Situation2: A customer brings a child’s wooden toy that is broken, and the carpenter should provide a repair quote
Story: It was just past midnight when my phone buzzed, jolting me awake. On the other end, my friend’s voice trembled, thick with tears. She’d just gotten terrible news about her father, and she needed someone to listen, to just be there. I sat up, heart pounding, trying to offer comfort, to be the friend she needed. But even as I murmured words of support, my mind kept drifting to the workshop. Earlier that evening, a customer had dropped off a child’s wooden toy, its arm snapped clean off. They’d asked for a repair quote by morning, saying it was their son’s favorite and his birthday was tomorrow. I could picture the little boy’s face, hopeful, waiting for his toy to be whole again. My friend’s sobs pulled me back, guilt gnawing at me. I wanted to give her my full attention, but the responsibility of the repair pressed on me. I felt torn, caught between being the friend she needed and the carpenter my customer expected. My hands shook as I tried to balance the phone, my words, and the weight of both worlds pressing in.
